en: The Ārṣeya Upaniṣad. Oṃ. The seers, wishing to engage in a theological debate (*brahmodya*), spoke to one another as they recited to each other. Among them, Viśvāmitra, considering himself the victor, said: "That which, between heaven and earth, pervades everything as if it were not pervading—just as this space [pervades]—and wherein from here and there they thunder, flash like lightning, and crash like thunderclaps—that is Brahman. This is its further explanation.

That they set him ablaze with fires; that they cause him to float away in water; that they press him down with heavy weights; that they bind him with leather thongs; that they strike him with iron clubs; that they pierce him with needles; that they drive him into the ground with stakes; that they split him apart with saws; that they smear him with clay; that they carve him with axes; that they plow him with ploughshares—thinking, "We shall not be able to do this," we would not dare to rule over him, nor would we ever transgress against him.

Jamadagni did not approve of this, thinking, "This [path] is indeed afflicted; for they approach it by going between these two [worlds]. This one is, as it were, excluded from both heaven and earth. He said, "This which is here is indeed the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); thus and so it is explained. [The other said,] "But I see its greatness here, namely that which is dependent upon this [space]. When one knows that which is dependent upon this and worships accordingly, he indeed becomes dependent upon it. One who worships what is dependent upon this without knowing this falls away and meets with affliction. Therefore, one should worship it in this very way.

The other asked him: "Which of these do you consider to be free from affliction? He replied to him: "That which they do not grasp as it were, nor perceive, nor reach—this world between heaven and earth. The further explanation of this is: "These shells of the cosmic egg that arise here and there do not fall, as it were; they do not hang down, as it were; they do not stumble, as it were; they do not turn back, as it were. Indeed, no one running toward them finds them, nor does anyone see them."
Regarding this, some say it is water alone; some say it is darkness; some say it is light; some say it is space; some say it is the supreme ether; and some say it is the Self.

Bharadvāja did not approve of this. "If you know everything here as being 'thus' and 'so'," they said, "that form of yours is incomplete. He replied, "This knowledge of yours is indeed distressed. Let us rather approach it by way of the two worlds, explaining it as 'thus' and 'so'. "But I worship its majesty alone," he said, "as that which is inherent here. "If one knows that which is inherent here and worships it accordingly, one becomes inherent right here."

He who here worships this [breath] as being thus dependent, without knowing it, becomes worse off, meets with calamity, and perishes. But he who worships this as being thus dependent reaches a full lifespan and becomes more prosperous. He who worships it as such—[it is he who truly attains these results].

The other asked him: "Which one do you consider to be free from affliction? He replied: "That which shines as light in this orb—whirling as it were, gleaming as it were, blazing as it were, radiating intensely as it were, licking [the sky] as it were—that alone is my Brahman. Its further explanation is this: that which reaches even to the furthest distances, that is indeed the perfected, that is the measured, according to how it has come forth; they behold it as the Self."

If one were to grasp this very thing by reaching out toward it—though it seems as if it were quivering, running away, leaping up, or clinging on—it does not actually come within reach. Thus, though it is near, it is as if far; though it is as if close at hand, it is distant. Indeed, no one at all attains its full majesty.

Gautama did not approve of this, saying: "That these people—the Puṇḍras, Suhmas, Kulumbhas, Daradas, and Barbaras—should look upon this [sun] as if it were something distressed or paralyzed, perceiving it only intermittently, is futile. "Indeed, they do not fail to perceive it; rather, they fall upon it all at once. "I, however, worship only its majesty: that golden person within this [disk], golden-hued, with a golden beard, shining as if ablaze even to the tips of his nails."

He who meditates upon him in this way stands preeminent over all beings; he reaches a full lifespan and becomes more prosperous. Indeed, he does not rise excessively above others. But he who, seeing him as rising excessively above others, meditates upon him in that way, becomes more wretched, falls away, and meets with calamity. However, he who knows him as rising not excessively above others and meditates accordingly, attains the supreme light, reaches a full lifespan, and becomes more prosperous—he who meditates upon him in this way.

The other asked him: "Which one do you consider to be unafflicted? He said to him: "These [flames] seem to quiver, as it were; they seem to flicker, as it were; they seem to rise up, as it were; they seem to be closest, as it were; they seem to be farthest, as it were; and they seem to be farthest, as it were, while being closest, as it were. "Even if one were to describe them in many ways, nothing at all can be apprehended; that is Brahman for me."

Vasiṣṭha, however, did not approve of this, saying: "When they approach these [waters] while they are thundering, they scatter them and move about in confusion; they gaze about as if at something unexpected. Truly, no one attains the further shore in this manner, as if lacking awareness. Those who are aware of it gaze within this very thing. "May we see and discern these through their greatness. He who, seeing these as indeed his own greatness, meditates upon them, attains greatness itself, reaches a full lifespan, and becomes more prosperous.

He who meditates upon these [days] as merely departing, and not as returning, becomes worse, falls apart, and dies. But he who meditates upon these as indeed returning, returns [to life], reaches a full lifespan, and becomes more prosperous.

The other asked him: "Which one do you consider to be free from affliction? [He replied: "That which, through its own nature, perceives 'this is thus, this is so,' as if it were great consciousness, as if it were a firm resolve; yet, when it is not 'this' nor 'that,' it perceives 'this is thus, this is so. This very Self is infinite, undecaying, and boundless. Indeed, O friend, it is neither external nor internal; it is all-knowing, of the nature of light, the remnant, the pervasive, the inner light, the consumer of all. It is the controller of all, the lord of all, encompassing all—nothing whatsoever reaches it."
Having praised Agni Vaiśvānara, who is superior and more excellent, who is to be invoked, who delights within all the worlds,
whom the Kuśikas have attained— he, born of Truth, has gone to the place of assembly.

In the tumultuous battles, we invoke that Indra—the victorious, the warrior, the most excellent, the all-conquering for the protection of people, the much-invoked, the one praised by the Ṛṣis, the possessor of all wealth. 2.
The invincible one, lying upon the ocean, expanding himself with supreme power.
Then they indeed attained it; having saluted him, they approached him, saying: "Homage to Agni! Homage to Indra! Homage to Prajāpati! Homage to Brahman! Homage to Brahman!"
Thus ends the Ārṣeya Upaniṣad.
